newsitem.title: FRANCE: No Burundi troops in Zaire, says Burundi minister.
newsitem.headline: No Burundi troops in Zaire, says Burundi minister.

text.p: Burundi Foreign Minister Luc Rukingama denied on Friday his country had sent troops into neighbouring Zaire to back rebels threatening to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko.

"The Zairean authorities have themselves admitted they have no proof there are Burundi forces in east Zaire. The truth is we have neither the intention nor any interest in meddling in the affairs of our neighbours," he told a news conference.
Zaire, whose troops are fighting an apparently losing battle against mostly Tutsi rebels advancing on four fronts, has accused Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of sending soldiers onto its territory.

"Frankly we have enough difficulties of our own without wanting to involve ourselves elsewhere," said Rukingama. He added that anti-government forces in Burundi launched their attacks from bases abroad, probably in Tanzania.
France, which has traditionally backed Mobutu, said on Thursday it was "paying special attention" to the presence of foreign troops in Zaire.
The United States on Wednesday said it had urged Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi to stay out of the fighting in east Zaire.
Paris said it agreed with Washington that the participation of foreign forces in the Zaire conflict would create "an extremely serious situation".

Rukingama made a scathing attack on United Nations observers in his country and the Amnesty International human rights group about a U.N. report of January 28 saying Burundi troops killed more than 1,000 people in violence involving the Tutsi-dominated army and the country's Hutu majority.
"I am saddened to tell you the work of the U.N. delegate in Burundi is extremely prejudicial. He circulates reports carrying non-verified information.
"There is a clear improvement in the security situation but, probably as a result, there is a campaign of demonisation of Burundi," he said.
Aid agencies say the Burundi government has grouped over 150,000 people in relocation camps in the past month and a report on Thursday said disease had killed 150 of them in one camp near Bujumbura.
Rukingama said government troops had committed "some excesses" under extreme provocation but had been punished. He added that there had "not been a single political murder in the past six months".
Rukingama spoke after meeting French Cooperation Minister Jacques Godfrain but he was not received by his French counterpart Herve de Charette.

Asked where his country stood on long-standing French suggestions that the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity should organise a conference on the explosive situation in the African Great Lakes area with strong West European input, he replied:

"We are favourable to all mechanisms of consultation that can be put into place on a national or regional level. The international community at large can come and help but the crux of the problem is in the concerned countries," he said.

Rukingama's visit preceded that of Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, expected in Paris on Tuesday. Museveni has also been invited for talks at the European Commission in Brussels, as has Kenyan President Daniel Arap Moi.
